# B Micah 1 — Extraction Digest
**Range:** raw lines 1610–2115 (cache local 1–506; formula: raw ≈ local + 1609)
**Source:** Nogalski, *The Book of Micah* (NICOT 2024)
**Coverage:** Text & Commentary I: Judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem (Mic 1:1–16) — superscription; theophany/judgment (1:2–7); prophetic lament and Shephelah warnings (1:8–16); theological afterword on Mic 1; endnotes supporting the chapter. Last local line reached: **506** (raw ≈ **2115**). Slice ends mid-footnote apparatus after n. 90 on Achzib/lmlk workshops.

## Claims

### C-B-01 — Three units of Micah 1
**Locus:** L1611–1613 / Mic 1:1–16 overview
**Quote/anchor:** "Micah 1 contains three interrelated units: the superscription (1:1), the introduction to the book in the form of a judgment oracle (1:2–7), and a prophetic lament over the Shephelah (1:8–16)."
**Claim:** Nogalski structures Mic 1 as three interrelated units: superscription (1:1); judgment-oracle introduction (1:2–7); prophetic lament over the Shephelah (1:8–16).
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-B-02 — Superscription contents and theme
**Locus:** L1613 / Mic 1:1
**Quote/anchor:** "The superscription provides the name of the prophet, the kings of Judah under whom the prophet lived, and the theme of the book (the fate of Samaria and Jerusalem)."
**Claim:** Nogalski holds that Mic 1:1 supplies prophet’s name, Judean kings of his time, and the book’s theme as the fate of Samaria and Jerusalem.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[samaria]], [[jerusalem]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-B-03 — Samaria as warning; Hezekiah/Assyrian setting of 1:8–16
**Locus:** L1613–L1617 / Mic 1:2–16
**Quote/anchor:** "the judgment oracle begins with a call to the nations, but then admonishes Jerusalem to learn a lesson from the fall of Samaria (722 BCE). … The pronouncements to the villages in 1:8–16 … evoke the impending attacks in the time of Hezekiah (701 BCE) when the Assyrian king solidifies control of the Levant and the coast."
**Claim:** Nogalski: 1:2–7 uses Samaria’s fall (722 BCE) to admonish Jerusalem; 1:8–16 proleptically warns Shephelah villages and evokes Sennacherib-era attacks under Hezekiah (701 BCE).
**Wiki targets:** [[samaria]], [[jerusalem]], [[hezekiah]], [[sennacherib]], [[micah]]

### C-B-04 — Exilic redaction linking Hosea, Amos, Zephaniah
**Locus:** L1619 / Mic 1:1 (composite/redaction)
**Quote/anchor:** "the king list and the thematic summary have been connected to an exilic redaction that joined Micah with Hosea, Amos, and Zephaniah. This combination of kings provides a patterned series of superscriptions, and the thematic summary at the end of 1:1 fashioned the first chapter into a warning to Jerusalem to learn from the overthrow of Samaria."
**Claim:** Nogalski reports scholarly connection of king list + thematic summary to an exilic redaction joining Micah with Hosea, Amos, and Zephaniah, patterning superscriptions and framing ch. 1 as a Samaria-to-Jerusalem warning.
**Wiki targets:** [[book-of-the-twelve]], [[hosea]], [[amos]], [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-B-05 — Contested integrity of 1:2–7; every verse claimed as insertion by someone
**Locus:** L1619–L1621 / Mic 1:2–7
**Quote/anchor:** "every verse in the “unit” has been claimed as an insertion by someone because it does not flow inherently with the surrounding text because a later editor inserted the verse."
**Claim:** Nogalski: authorship/homogeneity, logical flow, and date of 1:2–7 remain contested; portions of 1:2, 1:3–4, and 1:5–7 have been proposed as secondary, and every verse has been claimed as insertion by someone.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-B-06 — Mic 1:2 linked thematically to chs. 4–5 (nations judgment)
**Locus:** L1623–L1625 / Mic 1:2
**Quote/anchor:** "the thematic relationship between the judgment against the nations in 1:2 and the rest of Micah aligns the verse more closely with chapters 4–5 than with 1:3–7. … chapters 4–5 are widely considered postexilic expansions … and in this author’s opinion represent the latest block of texts in the book."
**Claim:** Nogalski: nations-judgment in 1:2 aligns better with Mic 4–5 than with 1:3–7; he regards chs. 4–5 as postexilic and the latest block in Micah.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]], [[book-of-the-twelve]]

### C-B-07 — 1:8–16 assumes some form of 1:2–7
**Locus:** L1627 / Mic 1:8–16
**Quote/anchor:** "1:8–16 appears to assume some form of 1:2–7, especially because 1:8 refers back to all this."
**Claim:** Nogalski treats 1:8–16 as presupposing some form of 1:2–7, with “this” in 1:8 referring back.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-B-08 — 1:8–16 structure: lament, Shephelah, Lachish/Moresheth, Sennacherib
**Locus:** L1629 / Mic 1:8–16
**Quote/anchor:** "The unit opens with a lament proper (1:8–9), spoken by the prophetic figure. Two sets of warnings ensue … villages in the Shephelah … (1:10–12) and … Lachish as an ominous warning … (1:13–16), including the prophet’s own hometown (Moresheth-Gath in 1:14). The mention of Lachish … suggest that the passage evokes the events of Sennacherib’s campaign in 701 BCE wherein he destroyed Lachish and laid siege to Jerusalem."
**Claim:** Nogalski structures 1:8–16 as prophet’s lament (1:8–9) then Shephelah warnings (1:10–12) and Lachish-centered warnings (1:13–16, incl. Moresheth-Gath), evoking Sennacherib’s 701 BCE campaign (Lachish destroyed; Jerusalem besieged).
**Wiki targets:** [[sennacherib]], [[jerusalem]], [[micah]], [[hezekiah]]

### C-B-09 — Superscription four pieces of information
**Locus:** L1641–L1645 / Mic 1:1
**Quote/anchor:** "This superscription provides four pieces of information: (1) the word event formula identifying the prophetic recipient; (2) the prophet’s hometown; (3) a list of three Judean kings communicating a time frame for Micah’s ministry; and (4) a thematic summary of the prophet’s message."
**Claim:** Nogalski parses Mic 1:1 into four components: word-event formula; hometown; three Judean kings; thematic summary of the message.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-B-10 — LXX “And” at start of superscription not in Judean Desert MSS
**Locus:** L1639 / Mic 1:1 text note a
**Quote/anchor:** "The LXX indicates a vav at the beginning of the superscription (“And the word of the Lord came”). None of the Hebrew or Greek manuscripts from the Judean Desert exhibits this reading. It thus appears to be a later addition or a loose translation."
**Claim:** Nogalski: LXX initial *vav* is absent from Judean Desert Hebrew/Greek witnesses; he treats it as later addition or loose translation.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-B-11 — Word-event formula: divine source and sanction of Micah
**Locus:** L1649 / Mic 1:1
**Quote/anchor:** "More profoundly, it affirms that what follows carries the weight of an encounter with the divine. It conveys Yahweh as the source of what follows and, simultaneously, sanctions Micah as the recipient of the message."
**Claim:** Nogalski: the word-event formula does not specify mode of reception (hearing/dream/vision) but asserts Yahweh as source and sanctions Micah as recipient.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-B-12 — Name Micah means “Who is like Yahweh?”
**Locus:** L1651 / Mic 1:1
**Quote/anchor:** "The name Micah (mîkāh) ends with yāh suffix in Hebrew, as is perhaps more evident in the fuller spelling of the name in Jer 26:18 (mîkāyāh). The name consists of the interrogative particle mî (“Who?”), the preposition k (“like”) and the abbreviation yāh (“Yahweh”). The name means “Who is like Yahweh?”"
**Claim:** Nogalski analyzes Micah as a theophoric name (mî + k + yāh) meaning “Who is like Yahweh?,” fuller form mîkāyāh in Jer 26:18.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-B-13 — Moresheth location; Moresheth-Gath; outsider to Jerusalem
**Locus:** L1653 / Mic 1:1, 1:14
**Quote/anchor:** "Moresheth was likely a village about twenty miles southwest of Jerusalem in the Shephelah, though its precise location has been a matter of long-standing debate. … In Mic 1:14, the same village is called Moresheth-Gath. … Identifying Moresheth as the hometown of Micah has long been interpreted to mean that the prophet was not part of the Jerusalemite inner circle of religious leaders."
**Claim:** Nogalski: Moresheth likely ~20 miles SW of Jerusalem in the Shephelah (location debated); called Moresheth-Gath in 1:14; hometown traditionally taken to mark Micah as outside Jerusalem’s religious-power circle (compared with Amos of Tekoa and Jeremiah of Anathoth).
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]], [[amos]]

### C-B-14 — Azekah as proposed hometown of Micah the Moreshite (Lipschits & Wöhrle)
**Locus:** L1949 (n. 10) / Mic 1:1 hometown debate
**Quote/anchor:** "See the recent contribution … by Oded Lipschits and Jakob Wöhrle, “Azekah—the Hometown of Micah the Moreshtite,” ZAW 135 (2023): 230–50. They show how ideas concerning the location of the prophet’s home were unduly influenced by Christian sources from a much later time, and they reinvigorate the suggestion of identifying Moresheth-Gath with Azekah…"
**Claim:** Nogalski cites Lipschits & Wöhrle (2023) reinvigorating identification of Moresheth-Gath with Azekah, arguing earlier locational ideas were unduly shaped by much later Christian sources.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-B-15 — Kings Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah: dates and career-length problem
**Locus:** L1655 / Mic 1:1
**Quote/anchor:** "Micah 1:1 mentions three Judean kings: Jotham (756–741 BCE), Ahaz (741–725 BCE), and Hezekiah (725–696 BCE). … The reigns of these three kings cover more than sixty years, and for Micah to have served during the reigns of all three kings, he would need to have served as a prophet for at least sixteen years (741–725 BCE)."
**Claim:** Nogalski gives reign dates for Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah and notes the chronological problem: spanning three kings covers >60 years; overlap of all three requires ≥16 years of prophetic service.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[hezekiah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-B-16 — Eighth-century material only in Mic 1–3; none securely from Jotham/Ahaz
**Locus:** L1655 / Mic 1:1; Mic 1–3
**Quote/anchor:** "most of the material that scholars assign to the eighth-century prophet appears only in the first three chapters of the book. … by most reckonings, the eighth-century material contained in Mic 1–3 relates to events in the time of Hezekiah’s reign. None of it can be reliably dated to the reigns of Jotham or Ahaz."
**Claim:** Nogalski reports critical consensus that eighth-century material is largely confined to Mic 1–3 and that none of it can be reliably dated to Jotham or Ahaz—only to Hezekiah-era events.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[hezekiah]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-B-17 — Preferred solution: kings list from exilic attachment to Hosea–Amos–Zephaniah
**Locus:** L1655 / Mic 1:1; Book of the Four / Twelve
**Quote/anchor:** "a second solution, and the one preferred in this commentary, is that the mention of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah was created or enhanced by editors in the exilic period as a means of creating a chronological framework when Micah was attached to the same scroll as Hosea and Amos (or Hosea, Amos, and Zephaniah)."
**Claim:** Nogalski prefers exilic editorial creation/enhancement of the three-king list to build a chronological frame when Micah was joined to Hosea and Amos (or Hosea, Amos, and Zephaniah).
**Wiki targets:** [[book-of-the-twelve]], [[hosea]], [[amos]], [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-B-18 — Hos 1:1 and Zeph 1:1 as chronological system with Mic 1:1
**Locus:** L1655 / Mic 1:1; Hos 1:1; Zeph 1:1
**Quote/anchor:** "Hosea 1:1 lists five kings: Uzziah … Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah … and Jeroboam II. … Zephaniah 1:1 completes this chronological system by tracing Zephaniah’s genealogy from Josiah … backward to the prophet’s great-great-grandfather Hezekiah. Likely, the three kings mentioned in Mic 1:1 were added in the exilic period when the four writings (Hosea, Amos, Micah, and Zephaniah) were joined to one another."
**Claim:** Nogalski: Hos 1:1’s king list and Zeph 1:1’s Hezekiah genealogy complete a chronological backbone; Mic’s three kings were likely added in the exilic joining of the Book of the Four.
**Wiki targets:** [[book-of-the-twelve]], [[hosea]], [[amos]], [[micah]], [[hezekiah]]

### C-B-19 — Spelling of Hezekiah links Hos 1:1 and Mic 1:1 (vs Zeph)
**Locus:** L1961 (n. 16) / Mic 1:1; Hos 1:1; Zeph 1:1
**Quote/anchor:** "Hos 1:1 and Mic 1:1 spell Hezekiah in ways that are otherwise almost unique in the rest of the Old Testament. This spelling distinguishes Hos 1:1 and Mic 1:1 from the spelling of Hezekiah used in Zeph 1:1. … it only appears 3 times as yĕḥizqiyyā (Mic 1:1; Hos 1:1; and Ezra 2:16)."
**Claim:** Nogalski (via Schart) notes the rare spelling yĕḥizqiyyā of Hezekiah in Hos 1:1 and Mic 1:1 (only thrice OT; also Ezra 2:16), distinct from Zeph 1:1’s spelling—supporting staged joining of the Four.
**Wiki targets:** [[hosea]], [[micah]], [[book-of-the-twelve]], [[hezekiah]]

### C-B-20 — Thematic clause “concerning Samaria and Jerusalem” anticipates 1:5–7; exilic
**Locus:** L1657–L1659 / Mic 1:1b
**Quote/anchor:** "a large percentage of Micah (1–3 and 4–7) concerns the fate of Jerusalem, but references to Samaria appear only in 1:5–7. This last clause in 1:1 thus anticipates the material in 1:5–7. Yet, careful analysis of 1:5–7 indicates that these verses were added during the exilic updating of Micah that connected early traditions of Micah with Hosea and Amos. … These verses warn Jerusalem to cease imitating the idolatry of the Northern Kingdom but presume Samaria’s destruction."
**Claim:** Nogalski: “concerning Samaria and Jerusalem” anticipates only 1:5–7; he dates those verses (and Samaria’s mention in 1:1) to exilic updating linking Micah to Hosea and Amos, warning Jerusalem after Samaria’s fall.
**Wiki targets:** [[samaria]], [[jerusalem]], [[hosea]], [[amos]], [[micah]]

### C-B-21 — Earliest superscription likely prophet + hometown only
**Locus:** L1659 / Mic 1:1
**Quote/anchor:** "Regarding the earliest form of Mic 1:1 prior to the addition of the kings and the reference to Samaria, one may logically and plausibly assume that the prophet’s identity was included along with the hometown, especially since it appears in 1:14."
**Claim:** Nogalski plausibly reconstructs the earliest Mic 1:1 as prophet’s identity + hometown (cf. 1:14), with kings and Samaria as later additions.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-B-22 — Structure of 1:2–7: call, theophany, warning
**Locus:** L1701 / Mic 1:2–7
**Quote/anchor:** "The unit begins with a call to attention to all the peoples of the world (1:2), followed by a theophany report (1:3–4), and a warning to Jerusalem and Judah concerning impending judgment (1:5–7)."
**Claim:** Nogalski outlines 1:2–7 as call to the peoples (1:2), theophany report (1:3–4), and warning of judgment on Jerusalem/Judah (1:5–7).
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-B-23 — Five interpretations of the nations in 1:2
**Locus:** L1701 / Mic 1:2
**Quote/anchor:** "Scholars have interpreted the nations as: (1) the object of judgment within a theophany report; (2) the witnesses to a warrior-king’s departure from his palace …; (3) witnesses in the trial scene that follows; (4) a rhetorical device in an oral performance of a prophetic preacher; or (5) the object of judgment that foreshadows chapters 4–5 that were appended to the book in the Persian period."
**Claim:** Nogalski inventories five scholarly options for the role of the nations in 1:2 (objects of judgment; witnesses of warrior departure; trial witnesses; rhetorical device; foreshadowing Persian-period chs. 4–5).
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-B-24 — ʿēd … b means “witness against,” not “among” (vs Fretheim/LXX)
**Locus:** L1721–L1723; L1741 / Mic 1:2
**Quote/anchor:** "The idiom ʿēd … b lines up best with the former, which means one should translate the phrase as “witness against you” since no other Old Testament text uses the phrase to mean “among.” … Willis … demonstrates that the Hebrew idiom in 1:2 only appears elsewhere in contexts where a witness accuses someone of something untoward."
**Claim:** Nogalski (following Willis) translates 1:2bα as Yahweh “witness against you” (not Fretheim’s “among you” via LXX); the idiom elsewhere marks accusation.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-B-25 — 1:2bα as redactional gloss anticipating Mic 4–5
**Locus:** L1725–L1741 / Mic 1:2
**Quote/anchor:** "when the gloss is added in 1:2bα (And the Lord Yahweh will be a witness against you), the location makes the nations the only possible antecedent. … This insertion is not an isolated gloss, but a redactional gloss that anticipates the themes of later portions of the book."
**Claim:** Nogalski reconstructs original theophany call as 1:2a + 1:2bβ (without 1:2bα); 1:2bα is a redactional gloss making the nations the object of judgment and anticipating later book themes (Mic 4–5).
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]], [[book-of-the-twelve]]

### C-B-26 — Text-critical: MT jussive vs LXX future of “will be” (wyhw)
**Locus:** L1683 / Mic 1:2 text note c
**Quote/anchor:** "The Greek verb is a future indicative (estai)… The Masoretes, however, pointed the Hebrew verb as a jussive (wîhî)… These two verbs reflect the same consonantal text in Hebrew (wyhw), so the unpointed source text of the Greek was not different."
**Claim:** Nogalski: MT jussive “let the Lord be” vs LXX future “will be” share consonants wyhw; divergence is pointing, not different unpointed source.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

**Locus:** L1683 / Mic 1:2 text note c
**Quote/anchor:** "in one Hebrew manuscript, 1Q 14, and one Greek manuscript, 8Ḥev 1, the divine name is written in an archaic Hebrew script … The result is visually stunning, particularly in 8Ḥev 1 since one does not expect to see Hebrew in a Greek text."
**Claim:** Nogalski notes archaic Hebrew script for the divine name in 1Q14 and Greek 8Ḥev 1 at this locus.

### C-B-28 — High places in 1:3 = mountains, not illicit cult poles of 1:5
**Locus:** L1751 / Mic 1:3–5
**Quote/anchor:** "Micah 1:5 portrays the high place(s) in a polemical fashion, similar to those places of illicit worship castigated in the Deuteronomistic History. By contrast, most scholars interpret high places in 1:3 as mountains on the basis of 1:4 and the language of theophanies in general. … The mountains (high places) in 1:3 are not the target of Yahweh’s judgment, they merely suffer as a result of Yahweh’s presence because they cannot bear his weight."
**Claim:** Nogalski: bāmôt in 1:3 are mountains overwhelmed by theophany weight, not the polemical illicit high places of 1:5 / DtrH.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-B-29 — 1:5–7: Samaria destroyed; Judah threatened with same; 722 vs 701
**Locus:** L1713 / Mic 1:5–7
**Quote/anchor:** "Micah 1:5–7 threaten Judah and Jerusalem with the same type of judgment experienced by Samaria (and the Northern Kingdom). As such, the verses presuppose Samaria’s destruction (722 BCE), but seem to treat that event as something in the recent past. Yet, scholars generally interpret 1:8–16 in light of Sennacherib’s campaign (701 BCE) some twenty years after Samaria’s destruction."
**Claim:** Nogalski: 1:5–7 presuppose Samaria’s 722 BCE fall as recent past and threaten Judah/Jerusalem with like judgment; 1:8–16 is generally read against Sennacherib 701 BCE (~20 years later).
**Wiki targets:** [[samaria]], [[jerusalem]], [[sennacherib]], [[micah]]

### C-B-30 — Jacob in 1:5b = Northern Kingdom vs Jacob = Judah elsewhere in Mic 1–3
**Locus:** L1761–L1763 / Mic 1:5
**Quote/anchor:** "Jeremias correctly notes … that 1:5b assumes that Jacob means the Northern Kingdom, that is, Israel. … this assumption runs counter to the times the phrase Jacob (or house of Jacob) is used in foundational material in Micah (3:1, 8–9; cf. 1:14–15; 2:7). All the other references to Jacob in Micah assume that Jacob refers to Judah."
**Claim:** Nogalski (with Jeremias): 1:5b equates Jacob’s sin with Samaria (Northern Kingdom), whereas other foundational Mic references use Jacob for Judah—a compositional tension.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[samaria]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-B-31 — High places chain: earth’s mountains → Jerusalem → berm (to 3:12)
**Locus:** L1771–L1775 / Mic 1:3–6; 3:12
**Quote/anchor:** "each successive reference to the high places (bāmōt) appears smaller. In the theophany (1:3–4), Yahweh tramples across the highest mountains of the earth… In 1:5… Is it not Jerusalem? … In 1:6, the farmer tills Jerusalem like a field and the high place turns into nothing more than a bump in the dirt…"
**Claim:** Nogalski traces a diminishing bāmôt chain from cosmic mountains (1:3–4) through Jerusalem as Judah’s high place (1:5) to a mere field berm (1:6), linking toward 3:12’s plowed-field imagery for Jerusalem.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-B-32 — 1:6 and 3:12 inclusio for Mic 1–3 as pre-4–7 written block
**Locus:** L1781 / Mic 1:6; 3:12
**Quote/anchor:** "1:6 indicates Samaria will become a heap (of rubble) in the field which reflects virtually the same language used of Jerusalem in 3:12. … 1:6 helps to create an inclusio between the first and last units of Mic 1–3, which in turn suggests that chapters 1–3 existed in written form before chapters 4–7 were incorporated into the book of Micah."
**Claim:** Nogalski: parallel “heap/rubble in the field” language in 1:6 (Samaria) and 3:12 (Jerusalem) forms an inclusio implying written Mic 1–3 before incorporation of chs. 4–7; composition not before Josiah’s reforms (622) and possibly after exilic Kings (~560).

### C-B-36 — Prophet (not Yahweh) laments naked and barefoot; “this” and “her”
**Locus:** L1839–L1839 / Mic 1:8–9

**Claim:** Nogalski: first-person lamenter of 1:8 is the prophet (not Yahweh of 1:6–7); “this” looks back to 1:3–7; “her wound” continues feminine personification of Samaria from 1:6–7.

### C-B-37 — Parallel to Isaiah’s naked-and-barefoot sign (Isa 20; 711 vs 701)
**Locus:** L1841 / Mic 1:8; Isa 20:2–4
**Quote/anchor:** "The only other time one finds the combination “naked and barefoot” in the Old Testament is Isa 20:2–4. … Isaiah 20 … response to an attack on Philistia by Sargon … in 711 BCE. … In 1:8, the prophet Micah speaks of walking naked and barefoot in response to an attack … from Sennacherib in 701 BCE. … Micah’s symbolic action mirrors that of Jerusalem’s most famous prophet of the day."
**Claim:** Nogalski treats Mic 1:8’s “naked and barefoot” as the only OT parallel to Isa 20:2–4, creating a twin symbolic action: Isaiah/Sargon–Ashdod 711 vs Micah/Sennacherib–Gath/Shephelah 701.

### C-B-38 — Jackals and ostriches: desolation imagery for Samaria/Jerusalem threat
**Locus:** L1843 / Mic 1:8b
**Quote/anchor:** "the prophet wails like howling jackals and screeching ostriches. … these two animals are frequently associated with deserted, nearly uninhabitable lands symbolizes the desolate state of Samaria which, in turn, accentuates the threat against Jerusalem."

### C-B-39 — 1:9b redactional: Samaria’s wound reaches Judah/Jerusalem; 2 Kgs 17 paradigm
**Locus:** L1845–L1847 / Mic 1:9
**Quote/anchor:** "Mic 1:9 draws on the content of 1:5–7 by assuming that Samaria’s destruction was caused by its idolatry and that Jerusalem’s imitation of Samaria’s behavior … threatens Jerusalem with the same fate as Samaria. … In all likelihood, 1:9 represents a redactional insertion to link the lament of 1:8 with the rhetorical unit of 1:10–16. … the theologizing of 1:9 reflects a periodization of the last two decades of the eighth century to convey theological ideas noticeably found in 2 Kgs 17:7–20."
**Claim:** Nogalski likely treats 1:9 as redactional, binding Samaria’s idolatry-caused fall (722) to the 701 lament/warnings and aligning with 2 Kgs 17’s theologizing of North then South.

### C-B-40 — Exilic updates in 1:9, 12: from 701 to 587 paradigm
**Locus:** L1823–L1825 / Mic 1:8–16 redaction
**Quote/anchor:** "short comments in 1:9, 12 reflect exilic theological interpretations … For most of these scholars these theologically driven comments presuppose knowledge that Jerusalem was destroyed by Babylon in 587 and intentionally evoke the events of 587 as well as 701 BCE. … an early source associated with Sennacherib’s attacks (most of 1:10–16 and at least some portion of 1:8–9) was updated to highlight the prophecy associated with Micah’s message of future judgment (which did not happen in 701 BCE, but ultimately came to pass in 587 BCE)."
**Claim:** Nogalski reports (and works with) a model: early Sennacherib-related source in 1:8–16* updated by exilic comments (esp. 1:9, 12) so that non-fall in 701 is reread toward 587 fulfillment.

**Locus:** L1857–L1891 / Mic 1:10

**Claim:** Nogalski: Mic 1:10 cites/echoes 2 Sam 1:20 (“Tell it not in Gath”) but recontextualizes Gath as Judean; *plš* puns Philistia; evoking Saul’s death/David’s rise, the unit threatens Jerusalem and the Davidic house.

**Claim:** Nogalski places Gath ~23 mi W of Jerusalem and Beth-Leaphrah ~20 mi (eastern Shephelah edge); Beth-Leaphrah = “house of dust,” punning the dust-rolling command.

**Locus:** L1893–L1899 / Mic 1:11–12

**Claim:** Nogalski catalogs town-name puns: Shaphir (“beautiful”) → nakedness/shame; Zenaan sound-play with “go forth” negated; Maroth (“bitter”) writhes for “good” while Yahweh’s calamity reaches Jerusalem’s gate.

**Locus:** L1903–L1905 / Mic 1:13

**Claim:** Nogalski: Lachish’s 701 fall and Sennacherib’s palace reliefs mark Assyrian threat; 1:13b (often treated as secondary with 1:5–7) calls Lachish “beginning of sin for Lady Zion” with Israel’s rebellions found there—link to Samaria-parallel theme debated among Allen, Jeremias, Sweeney, Wolff.

**Locus:** L1907 / Mic 1:14
**Quote/anchor:** "The metaphors and paronomasia in 1:14 essentially combine to portray the divorce of Moresheth-Gath, the prophet’s hometown (1:1). While the Assyrians did not totally destroy Jerusalem, its fortified towns and its territory were largely destroyed… Prophetic books routinely stress judgment in the opening chapters and end with words of hope… Mic 1–3 culminates with the pronouncement that Jerusalem will be plowed under… (3:12). ### C-B-51 — ʿî “heap” hapax: BHK/BHS/BHQ shift on LXX hopōrophuakion

BHK3 notes that the LXX renders the word ʿî … as hopōrophuakion, which translates as “hut”… Looking at these three critical editions demonstrates a dramatic shift in how scholars deal with variant readings in the LXX. They have become much less confident that such variations automatically point to a different text…"
**Claim:** Nogalski uses ʿî (“heap of rubble”) as a case study: BHK emends from LXX “hut,” BHS notes without preferring, BHQ ignores as paraphrastic—illustrating decreased confidence that LXX variants automatically reflect a different Hebrew *Vorlage*.

### C-B-52 — LXX treatment of Moresheth-Gath and Achzib in 1:14
**Locus:** L1817–L1821 / Mic 1:14 text notes c–e
**Quote/anchor:** "The LXX does not name Moresheth-Gath as the town, but merely has Gath (get). Instead, the LXX translates the unpointed Hebrew conanants (šlwḥym) with “inheritance”… The LXX eliminates the “town” name from the phrase houses of Achzib … and translates that phrase as “vain houses”… The name of the town thus disappears in the LXX while two Greek synonyms for “vain” appear…"
**Claim:** Nogalski: LXX loses Moresheth (reads inheritance of Gath) and eliminates Achzib as place-name, doubling “vain/empty” synonyms—working from a text close to MT but muddling sense via translation strategy.
